### Output:

```
PMID 27491499
TITLE Renal assessment using CKD-EPI equation is useful as an early predictor of contrast- induced nephropathy in elderly patients with cancer.
JOURNAL Journal of geriatric oncology
DATE 2017 None
ABSTRACT To assess respective roles of serum creatinine (SCr) alone and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) as an early predictor for contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) in elderly patients with cancer. eGFR of 348 patients at 65years or older with malignancy who underwent contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) were calculated. eGFR was calculated based on the following three equations: Chronic Kidney Disease Epidemiology Collaboration equation (CKD-EPI); Modification of Diet in Renal Disease Study (MDRD); Cockcroft-Gault (CG). CIN was subdivided into two groups: CIN25% (SCr increase >25% but ≤0.5mg/dl), and CIN0.5 (SCr increase >0.5mg/dl). The occurrence and clinical outcomes of CIN were determined according to SCr and eGFR. After CECT, CIN occurred in 50 (14.4%) patients, including 33 CIN25% patients and 17 CIN0.5 patients. CIN0.5 was significantly correlated with prolonged hospitalizations and increased in-hospital mortality, but not CIN25%. Despite SCr<1.5mg/dl, preexisting renal insufficiency (RI) was observed in 47 (13.5%) patients based on CKD-EPI equation, 50 (14.4%) patients based on MDRD equation, and 144 (41.4%) patients based on CG formula. In preexisting RI, the prevalence of CIN0.5 had an odds ratio of 15.02 (5.24 to 43.07) based on CKD-EPI equation, 13.73 (4.81 to 39.20) based on MDRD equation, and 5.03 (1.60 to 15.75) based on CG formula. In elderly patients with cancer who visit the emergency department, renal assessment before CECT using CKD-EPI equation was superior to SCr alone, MDRD equation, or CG formula in predicting the occurrence of CIN related CECT.

```

**Yes—CKD-EPI appears useful for early risk prediction in this population.** A 2017 study of 348 cancer patients aged 65 or older undergoing contrast-enhanced CT found that 50 (14.4%) developed contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN). Among patients whose serum creatinine was below 1.5 mg/dL, CKD-EPI identified pre-existing renal insufficiency in 47 patients (13.5%). That subgroup had higher odds of a creatinine rise greater than 0.5 mg/dL after contrast (OR 15.02, 95% CI 5.24–43.07). The reported association was stronger than with MDRD (OR 13.73) or Cockcroft–Gault (OR 5.03), and CKD-EPI was reported as more useful than serum creatinine alone. This larger creatinine rise was also associated with longer hospitalization and higher in-hospital mortality. [PMID: 27491499](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27491499/)

**Caveat:** This conclusion rests on a single study; the abstract does not establish external validation or provide standard predictive-performance measures such as sensitivity, calibration, or discrimination. CKD-EPI should therefore be viewed as a useful pre-scan risk-assessment aid—not a guarantee that CIN will occur or proof that contrast caused subsequent kidney injury.

FINAL DECISION: YES
